parts.title: My grandmother's cafe
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
My grandmother opened her cafe forty years ago, on a corner near the market. At first, it had only four tables, and she made everything herself: the soup, the sandwiches and the apple cake that people still talk about.

When I was a child, I spent every summer there. I washed cups, carried plates and listened to the customers. There was an old man who came every morning at eight and ordered a black coffee, and a group of students who argued about films for hours. My grandmother knew every name, and she remembered how everybody liked their drinks.

Last year, she became ill and thought about selling the cafe. I did not want that to happen, so I took a break from university to help. It was harder than I had expected. I got up at five to bake, and my feet hurt by the afternoon.

Now business is better than ever. We have added a small shelf of second-hand books, and customers can borrow one while they drink their coffee. My grandmother visits every day, sits at her favourite table and tells me that the cake is not as good as hers. She is probably right.

questions.explanation: People still talk about her apple cake.

parts.title: A short history of coffee
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Coffee has a long and interesting history. [1] According to an old story, a farmer in Ethiopia noticed that his goats became very lively after eating the red berries of a certain bush.

At first, people ate the berries or chewed the leaves. [2] Slowly, the habit of drinking coffee spread across the Arab world, where the first coffee houses opened.

In the seventeenth century, traders brought coffee to Europe. [3] Many people thought it was a dangerous drink, but soon cafes appeared in every big city.

These cafes became meeting places. [4] Writers, artists and business people spent hours there, talking and reading the news.

Today, coffee is one of the most traded goods in the world. [5] For many people, a day cannot begin without a cup.
sentences: Tea is much more popular in some countries.
The beans are still picked by hand on most farms.
Over two billion cups are drunk every day.
She was the first woman in her town to own one.
It was a completely new taste for most of them.
People could hear new ideas and share them for the price of a cup.
Nobody knows exactly who first discovered it.
Later, someone had the idea of making a hot drink from the beans.

gaps.explanation: Nobody knows who discovered it; the next sentence gives an old story.
People first ate berries; later they made a hot drink from the beans.
It was a new taste; the next sentence says many people thought it was dangerous.
Cafes were meeting places where people shared ideas; the next sentence lists writers and artists.
Billions of cups are drunk every day; the next sentence says people cannot start the day without one.

parts.title: A talk by a cafe owner
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: owner
turns.text: Welcome to my cafe, everybody. I am Aldis, and I started this business five years ago. Before that, this building was a shoe shop for twenty years, and my uncle had a bakery here, but both closed. I want to tell you a little about how we work. We open at half past seven on weekdays, because many people come before work. On Saturdays and Sundays we open later, at half past eight. Some of you have asked for seven, but the bakers aren’t here that early. Now, the food. The most popular cake is the lemon cake. Years ago it was chocolate, and my own favourite is carrot, but every day we sell out of lemon before lunch. All our cakes are baked here. We care about where things come from. The milk comes from a farm ten kilometres away. The eggs come from a farm only two kilometres from here, and the flour comes from a mill about thirty kilometres away, near the river. We like to keep it local, because the food tastes better and the farmers are my friends. We also have events. The book club meets on Wednesday evenings. Don’t confuse it with the knitting group, which meets on Thursdays, or the music night, which is on the last Friday of the month. Everyone is welcome at all of them, and they are free, so you only pay for what you eat and drink. Bring a friend if you are shy. Finally, a word about our staff. Many students work here at weekends. People who work on weekdays get a free breakfast, but those who work at the weekend get a free lunch, because they stay longer and have more customers. It’s a small thank you. Now please come in, have a look around, and try a slice of cake.

gaps.explanation: Aldis started five years ago; the shoe shop lasted twenty years before that.

gaps.prompt: On weekdays the cafe opens at half past ___
gaps.explanation: Weekdays start at half past seven; weekends open at half past eight, and seven was asked for but is too early.

gaps.prompt: The most popular cake is the ___ cake
gaps.explanation: Chocolate was popular years ago and carrot is his favourite, but lemon sells out every day.

gaps.prompt: The milk comes from a farm ___ kilometres away
gaps.explanation: The eggs are two kilometres away and the flour thirty; the milk farm is ten kilometres away.

gaps.prompt: The book club meets on ___ evenings
gaps.explanation: The knitting group is on Thursdays and the music night on Fridays; the book club meets on Wednesdays.
Weekday workers get a free breakfast; weekend workers get a free lunch.

parts.title: An interview with a tea taster
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Dante, you are a professional tea taster. Who encouraged you as a boy?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: My teacher gave me good marks, but he didn’t really care about tea. And my father only drank coffee, and he laughed at me in the beginning. It was my grandmother. She had a big kitchen with forty jars of tea, and every Sunday she asked me to smell three of them and guess what they were. I was seven, and I loved the game.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you note about each tea?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Not the price or the size of the leaf, that’s for the buyers, who count money. And I don’t care much about the name or the country when I taste. I write down three things: the colour, the smell and the flavour. Then I compare them with my notes from last year. Good tea has a very clear story in those three words.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why do you spit the tea out?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s a surprise for visitors. It isn’t too hot, because we let it cool, and it isn’t old, it’s fresh from the factory. The reason is simple. I taste up to two hundred cups a day. If I swallowed them all, I wouldn’t sleep at night, with so much caffeine in my body.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do people do wrong when they make tea?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A lot of people put too much milk in, and that’s just taste, not a mistake. Another idea is that water must be cold, which is nonsense, it needs to be hot. The real mistake is to leave the bag in too long. After four minutes the tea gets bitter, and then they add sugar to fix it. Take the bag out and enjoy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How do you like your tea at home?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Very simple. I’m not a fan of sweet tea, and I find lemon covers the taste. At home I drink it with a drop of milk, nothing else. I taste complicated flavours all day at work, so I want something quiet when I finish.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is your advice for someone who wants to become a taster?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Many people say you should study chemistry, and it helps, but it’s not essential. Travelling is great, but I started without it. If I had to choose one thing, it’s patience. Smell, wait, try again. You need years to learn, and nobody can hurry it.
